title: Families parenting and commitment
objectives: Explain how care, safety and respect can support a child.
Identify adult parenting tasks in an invented family.
Explain a safe commitment and a route to adult help.
vocabulary: People linked by care or family ties. Families can have different forms.
The work adults do to care for a child and help the child grow safely.
A task or duty a person is expected to carry out.
An agreement or choice to keep giving time and care. It must not mean accepting harm.
Treating a person with care and taking their rights and boundaries seriously.

model.title: A changed collection plan
model.story: In an invented family, one parent cares for a child. The parent has to change a collection plan. The parent tells the agreed adult, checks that the child will be with a safe adult and explains the change calmly. The child can ask questions. The adult sorts out the plan.
model.reasoning: The parent shows care by making a safe plan and giving clear information. The adult is responsible for the child getting safe care. A change does not mean that care has ended. The child does not have to solve the adult problem. A safe commitment includes keeping promises where possible and explaining a safe change.

cases.title: Care across two homes
cases.story: A child in an invented family spends time in two homes. The adults agree who will help with a health appointment and who will collect the child. They share the plan without asking the child to carry messages. They listen when the child has a question.
questions: Which two actions show care or responsibility?
Why is it helpful for the adults to share the plan?
Would this family need the same shape as the model family to show commitment? Explain.
cases.answer: Agreeing care for the appointment, arranging collection, sharing the plan and listening all show care or responsibility. Adults communicating directly can reduce uncertainty and keeps adult tasks with adults. The child is not a messenger or referee. Families can have different forms and still provide safe, steady care. The quality of care cannot be judged from the number of homes or adults alone.

cases.title: A relative gives care
cases.story: In another invented family, a relative is the main carer. The carer prepares food, checks that the child has what they need and asks a trusted adult for help with a new routine. The child is offered a small, age-suitable choice about their own activity. The carer stays responsible for safety.
questions: Which tasks belong to the adult?
Does asking for safe support show a lack of commitment? Give a reason.
How can the adult listen to the child while keeping responsibility?
cases.answer: Food, safe care, checking needs and arranging support are adult tasks. Asking for suitable support can help the carer meet the child's needs; it does not by itself show a lack of commitment. Listening to an age-suitable choice respects the child. The adult must still make safe arrangements. A child may have small suitable tasks but must not take over the adult's caring responsibility.

cases.title: A promise that needs help
cases.story: In a third invented family, an adult says that commitment means a child must keep quiet about anything that makes the child feel unsafe. The child is unsure. A trusted member of staff is available for a private talk. The safeguarding lead can help with the concern.
questions: Is keeping quiet about feeling unsafe a safe meaning of commitment?
Which safe adult route could the child use?
What could happen if the first trusted adult is not available?
cases.answer: No. Care or commitment never requires silence about harm, fear or safety concerns. The child can speak privately to a trusted adult or the safeguarding lead. If the first adult is unavailable or does not help, the child can try another trusted adult or ask to reach the safeguarding lead. If there is immediate danger, seek adult help straight away through the urgent procedure. The child is not at fault and does not need to investigate, confront anyone or prove a concern before asking for help.

hinge.question: An invented carer asks a safe adult for help so a child is cared for. Which answer fits?
options: A. Asking for support always shows a lack of commitment.
B. Safe support can help the carer meet the child's needs.
C. The child must take over all the adult tasks.
hinge.reason: Commitment can include safe support. The adults remain responsible for meeting the child's needs.
hinge.parallel_question: A family changes a plan and explains the new safe arrangement. Must this mean the family no longer cares?
parallel_options: A. No. A safe change can still show care and commitment.
B. Yes. Every plan must stay the same even if it is unsafe.
hinge.parallel_reason: Care includes adapting safely, keeping the child informed and checking that needs are met.

Supported: Use the word bank and visible model. In the two-homes story, choose two care actions: adults share the plan; the child must sort out the adults' disagreement; adults arrange safe collection. Point, say or record the two care actions.
Use the frame: The adult is responsible for ___. Asking a safe adult can help because ___. Match food, care and collection to adult responsibility in the relative story.
For the unsafe-promise story, choose telling a trusted adult or keeping quiet. Complete: The child could ask ___ for help. If that adult is not there, ___.
Independent: Read the two-homes story. Identify two care actions and explain how they help the child. Explain why family form alone does not show how safe or caring a family is.
Read the relative story. Distinguish the adult's duties from the child's small choice. Explain why safe support can help a carer keep a commitment.
Read the unsafe-promise story. Explain why commitment cannot require silence about safety. Give a trusted-adult route and a fallback if the first adult cannot help.
Aspire: Compare the changed-collection model and the two-homes story. Identify a shared caring action and explain why different family forms can meet the same need.
For the relative story, weigh two options: the carer asks for safe support, or the child takes over the adult tasks. Explain which option keeps care and responsibility in the right place.

For the unsafe-promise story, explain the limit of commitment. Adapt the help route when the first adult is unavailable. Give a reason without adding personal details or asking the child to investigate.

evidence_rows: Identifies two caring actions and does not rank families by their form.
Places caring duties with adults and explains how safe support can help.
Rejects secrecy about safety and gives a trusted adult or safeguarding lead route plus a fallback.
misconceptions: Only one family form can provide good care.
Family forms differ. Care, safety and respect matter in every family. A family label alone cannot show the quality of care.
Commitment means staying silent or coping alone.
Safe commitment can include asking for support, changing a plan and setting boundaries. It never requires accepting harm or keeping a safety concern secret.
teaching_points: Families take different forms. Safe care and respect matter in each form.
Adults are responsible for a child's care, safety and needs. Children are not responsible for fixing adult problems.
Commitment can mean reliable care, keeping safe promises and explaining changes. Asking for support can help.
A promise must never block help about safety. A trusted adult or the safeguarding lead can help; try another trusted adult if needed.
